Here’s a concise, ready-to-use summary of the full 12-week plan. It combines the strength program (4 days/week), the optional cardio plan (2–3 days/week), the Saturday finisher ideas, the mobility routine, and the nutrition basics we discussed. The plan is written to be delivered to a client or printed for reference. If you want, I can convert this into a calendar with week-by-week workouts and a one-page printable sheet.

Overall structure
- Duration: 12 weeks
- Training days: 4 strength days per week (A, B, C, D), with a possible 5th optional mobility/tech day or active recovery
- Cardio: 2–3 home cardio sessions per week on non-consecutive days or after strength sessions
- Saturday finisher: optional fun capstone sessions to finish the week
- Mobility: daily or near-daily 15–20 minute routine (adjust to schedule)
- Nutrition: protein-focused plan with a modest caloric surplus on training days, adjusted every 4 weeks

Weekly schedule (typical, can be adapted)
- Monday: Strength - Session A (Upper Body Push + Pull Balance)
- Tuesday: Cardio - Option 1 or 2 (phase-aligned)
- Wednesday: Strength - Session B (Lower/Full-Body with Push Emphasis)
- Thursday: Cardio or Mobility/Recovery - Option 3 or light mobility
- Friday: Strength - Session C (Push-Pull Strength Circuit)
- Saturday: Finisher Day - rotate among Options A–D
- Sunday: Rest or Mobility/Recovery

Phase progression
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Foundation and technique
  - Focus on learning patterns, establishing bracing, scapular control, basic volume
  - Main lifts: bodyweight squats, hinge patterns, incline/floor push-ups, inverted rows
  - Cardio: 2 sessions/week, low to moderate intensity; emphasis on form
  - Mobility: daily 15–20 minutes; emphasis on thoracic mobility and hips

- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Volume buildup and push intensity introduction
  - Push intensity increases (as outlined in Week-by-Week Phase 2 plan)
  - Tempo and paused reps introduced to increase time under tension
  - Main lifts shift to more sets/reps with associated tempo
  - Cardio: maintain 2–3 sessions/week; slight progression in duration or intervals
  - Finisher: rotate through Saturdays to maintain engagement

- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Intensity and technique refinement
  - Tempo continues (3-0-3 or similar)
  - Isometric holds and sticking-point work added
  - Pull/push balance maintained; progression focuses on controlling heavier loads
  - Cardio: 2–3 sessions/week with spaced intervals or tempo work
  - Mobility: emphasis on sustaining range and joint health under higher workloads

- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Peak strength and consolidation
  - High effort with low-to-moderate reps, aiming near technical failure with proper form
  - Maintain balance of pushing/pulling to protect shoulders
  - Cardio: maintain volume but avoid over-fatigue on long strength days
  - Mobility: maintain and tune for recovery; reduce stiffness and ensure full ROM

Core exercise template (per phase)
- Push basics:
  - Incline push-ups (Phase 1) → Floor push-ups (Phase 1/2 transition) → Dumbbell/kettlebell floor press or incline press (Phase 2+)
  - Tempo: Phase 2 2-0-2 or 3-0-2; Paused reps in Phase 3
- Pull basics:
  - Inverted rows or door-frame rows (early) → Pull-ups/ Chin-ups as able (Phase 1–4)
  - Tempo: controlled 2-0-2; add eccentric emphasis in Phase 2/3
- Squat/hinge basics:
  - Bodyweight squats (Phase 1) → Goblet squats with dumbbell/kettlebell (Phase 2+)
  - Hip hinges: glute bridges, hip thrusts; progress to dumbbell RDLs or KB deadlifts if equipment available
- Core/bracing:
  - Hollow holds, dead bugs, planks, side planks; progressive time under tension
- Conditioning:
  - Cardio options depend on space; use interval-style or tempo-based cardio as described

Finisher days (Saturday)
- Option A: 15–20 min playful circuit
- Option B: 15–25 min skill/mobility and control
- Option C: 15–18 min game-style rounds
- Option D: 15–20 min bar-guided rounds
- Aim: low-stress, enjoyable, reinforce movement quality and accountability

Mobility routine (15–20 minutes daily or 4–6 days/week)
- Warm-up: Cat-Cow, Thread-the-Needle, Arm circles, Hip circles
- Thoracic spine openers
- Shoulders and chest neutrality
- Scapular stability and wall slides
- Hip mobility and squat readiness
- Ankle and calf mobility
- Breathing and core bracing
- Cool-down: gentle stretches and relaxation
- Integration: use on non-training days as a dedicated routine or after workouts

Nutrition framework (baseline)
- Protein: 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight per day
- Fat: 0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight per day
- Carbs: fill remaining calories around workouts
- Calories: start with maintenance + 250–350 kcal on training days; adjust every 4 weeks
- Meal pattern: 3 main meals + 1–2 snacks; pre/post-workout nutrition aligned with workouts
- Hydration: 2–3 liters/day; electrolytes if needed
- Food quality: prioritize whole foods; balance micronutrients; limit highly processed foods
- Special considerations: vegetarian/vegan adjustments; intolerance considerations

Weighting and progression reminders
- Reps and sets: Week 1–3 use moderate reps; Week 4–6 add sets/reps; Week 7–9 emphasize tempo and control; Week 10–12 push toward higher effort
- Pull-ups: progress with negatives, assisted variations, or mixed with rows as needed
- Tempo and pauses: escalate to 3-second descent/paused reps in Phase 3
- Recovery: keep rest between sets roughly 60–90 seconds; 2–3 minutes for heavier pushing or pull work

Tracking and accountability
- Training log: exercise, sets, reps, tempo, RIR/effort
- Body metrics: weekly weight, body measurements as desired
- Check-ins: monthly review of technique, push/pull balance, and progress toward goals
- Adjustments: calories up/down based on weight progress; adjust protein to maintain target

Safety and troubleshooting
- Technique first: slow, controlled movements; avoid grinding form
- Pain vs. fatigue: differentiate; pain should stop progress and be evaluated
- Mobility integration: consistent daily mobility supports performance and recovery
- Noise considerations and space: choose floor-friendly movements and adapt to apartment constraints

If you want, I can convert this into:
- A week-by-week printable schedule with exact exercises, sets, reps, and tempos
- A 12-week calendar view (color-coded by phase)
- A client-facing one-page summary including the four weekly workout blocks, finisher options, cardio, and mobility

Tell me your client’s height/weight (for precise nutrition alignment), preferred equipment (if any beyond the doorway bar), and how many days per week you plan to train so I can tailor the final printable templates and exact week-by-week detail.

Great. Below is a structured 12-week strength program for a 27-year-old beginner training at home with only a yoga mat and a doorway pull-up bar. The plan emphasizes progressive overload, technique, and consistency while staying practical for a small flat. It includes weekly structure, exercise selection, sets/reps, progression cues, and brief nutrition/recovery guidance. If you have any constraints (time per session, injury history, or specific goals), tell me and I can tailor further.

Overview
- Frequency: 4 training days per week
  - 2 lower/upper split days (alternate) + 2 full-body conditioning/skill days
  - Optional 5th day for mobility or active recovery if desired
- Intensity progression: start with lighter loads focusing on technique; gradually increase reps, then load as technique solidifies
- Repertoire uses only: bodyweight exercises, isometric holds, and the doorway pull-up bar
- Progression principles: weekly micro-progressions in reps/sets and resistance (via tempo and range of motion), and eventually adding isometrics or tempo variations for increased stimulus with minimal equipment

Weekly structure (typical week)
- Day A: Upper Body Strength (push/pull emphasis)
- Day B: Lower Body Strength
- Day C: Full-Body Strength & Skill
- Day D: Posterior Chain & Core + Mobility
- 1–2 rest days or active recovery

Phases
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Foundation and technique
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Build up volume and introduce progressive overload
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Increase intensity with tempo/hold variations and a few load progressions
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Peak strength building with refined technique and higher effort

Equipment note
- Doorway pull-up bar: use for pull-ups/chin-ups as soon as form allows; you can also do hanging holds and scapular hangs.
- No extra weights: use tempo, isometrics, and incline variations to modulate difficulty.
- Mat: for comfort during floor exercises and core work.

Program details

Phase 1, Weeks 1–3 (foundation, technique)
Goals: establish baseline, learn hinge, squat, push, pull patterns; build work capacity; master proper bracing and scapular control.

Session A (Upper Body Strength)
- Warm-up: 5–8 minutes light cardio (marching, stepping in place), dynamic shoulder/opener movements (arm circles, banded if available; with no band, pendulum swings)
- Push-up progressions (choose level by ability):
  - Week 1–2: incline push-ups on a table or bench (hands on bench) or knees on floor; 3 sets of 8–10 reps
  - Week 3: incline push-ups progressing toward floor; 3 sets of 8–12 reps
- Row progressions (using door frame or floor plank row):
  - Inverted row under pull-up bar if possible: feet on floor, body at an angle beneath bar; or doorframe body rows (hands on bar, body angled). Start with 3 sets of 6–8 reps
  - If too hard, perform a Y-push/push-up plus isometric scapular squeeze: 3 sets of 8–10 seconds holds at a mid-squeeze
- Shoulder stability: standing scapular push-ups or wall slides (3 sets of 8–12)
- Core: dead bug or hollow hold (3 sets of 20–30 seconds)
- Finisher: 2 rounds of 30 seconds hollow hold + 8 push-ups (as needed)

Session B (Lower Body Strength)
- Warm-up: dynamic hips, hips hinge movement, ankle mobility
- Squat pattern: bodyweight squats focusing on depth and bracing
  - Week 1–2: bodyweight squats 3–4 sets of 10–12
  - Week 3: introduce goblet-like hold with a household object if available; 3–4 sets of 10–12
- Hip hinge: hip thrusts with glute bridge (2–3 sets of 12–15)
- Step-ups: onto a stable chair or low platform; 3 sets of 8–10 per leg
- Single-leg balance: (unipedal stance) 2 sets of 20–30 seconds per leg
- Core: side plank (2–3 sets per side, 20–40 seconds)
- Mobility: 2–3 minutes hamstring/calf stretches

Session C (Full-Body Strength & Skill)
- Warm-up: 5–8 minutes light cardio + movement prep
- Pull-up/push-up complex:
  - If bar usable: static hangs 15–20 seconds, 2 sets; assisted pull-up attempts (if possible) 3 sets of 3–5 reps
  - Push-ups: incline for week 1–2; floor push-ups by week 3 if ready; 3 sets of 6–10
- Lower body: lunges or split squats (forward or reverse)
  - 3 sets of 8–10 per leg
- Core: dead bug variations or farmer hold if available (3 sets of 20–30 seconds)
- Conditioning finisher: 3 rounds of 20 seconds per exercise: squat hold, push-up hold, jumping or step-downs (as tolerated)

Session D (Posterior Chain & Mobility)
- Warm-up: light cardio 5 minutes
- Glute bridge variations: single-leg glute bridge 3 sets of 8–12 per side
- Hamstring emphasis: lying or seated leg curls using bodyweight (3 sets of 10–12)
- Superman or bird dog: 3 sets of 8–12 reps
- Hip hinge practice: deadlift pattern with hips back and chest up (bodyweight)
- Core: rKCplanks or RKC planks 2–3 sets of 20–40 seconds
- Mobility: 10 minutes guided mobility focusing on hips, shoulders, thoracic spine

Phase 2, Weeks 4–6 (volume progression, moderate intensity)
Adjusts: increase reps, add one more set, start controlled tempo to increase time under tension, and introduce vertical pulling with the bar.

Session A
- Push-ups: 4 sets of 8–12
- Inverted rows or door-frame rows: 4 sets of 8–12
- Shoulder control: 3 sets of 6–8 scapular pull-ups or 8–12 wall slides
- Core: 3 sets of 20–30s hollow hold
- Optional: negative pull-ups (eccentric) if bar allows: 3 sets of 3–5 seconds descent

Session B
- Squats: 4 sets of 10–12
- Split squats: 3–4 sets of 8–10 per leg
- Hip hinges/glute bridges: 3–4 sets of 12–15
- Calf raises (on a step, if possible): 3 sets of 12–15
- Core: side planks 2–3 sets per side

Session C
- Pull-ups/Push-ups complex: 4 sets of 6–8 reps (or as many as possible with good form)
- Bulgarian split squat (using chair): 3–4 sets of 8–10 per leg
- Floor leg raises or hanging knee raises (if bar usable): 3–4 sets of 8–12
- Glute bridges with march or single-leg progressions: 3 sets of 8–12 per leg

Session D
- Glute-focused posterior chain: single-leg hip thrusts 3–4 sets of 8–12 per leg
- Hamstring practice: glute-ham raises if feasible, or Nordic hamstring progressions (as able)
- Core: planks and anti-rotation (side-to-side) 3 sets of 20–40 seconds
- Mobility: 12–15 minutes focusing on thoracic mobility and shoulder opening

Phase 3, Weeks 7–9 (intensity and technique refinement)
- Add tempo: 3–0–3 tempo (3 seconds down, 0 pause, 3 seconds up) for key lifts
- Increase difficulty of push/pull as bar allows (strict form)
- Introduce isometric holds at sticking points during squats and pull-ups

Session A
- Push-ups: 4–5 sets of 6–12 with tempo 3-0-3
- Bar pull-ups or rows: 4–5 sets of 6–10 with controlled tempo
- Shoulder work: isometric holds at top of press or scapular holds 3 sets of 15–20 seconds
- Core: hollow body hold 3 sets of 25–40 seconds

Session B
- Front/Back squats alternatives using tempo: 4 sets of 6–10
- Split squats with pause: 3–4 sets of 6–8 per leg
- Hip hinge: 4 sets of 8–12
- Core: rKC planks or side planks with reach 3 sets of 20–40 seconds

Session C
- Pull-up/push-up ladder: start with 2–3 reps, add one rep per set until near failure
- Bulgarian split squats with tempo: 4 sets of 6–8 per leg
- Leg raises or hanging knee raises: 4 sets of 8–12
- Anti-rotational core: Pallof press variations if possible (with band substitute or isometric hold)

Session D
- Posterior chain emphasis: single-leg Romanian deadlift progressions (bodyweight), 3–4 sets of 8–12 per leg
- Glute bridges with tempo: 4 sets of 8–12
- Core: 3 sets of 20–30 seconds of side planks

Phase 4, Weeks 10–12 (peak strength and consolidation)
- Focus on reaching higher effort with sound technique
- Maintain volume but push close to reps in reserve (RIR 0–1)
- Emphasize consistency, technique, and recovery

Session A
- Push-ups/press complex: 4–5 sets of 5–8 with strict form
- Pull-ups/rows: 4–5 sets of 6–8
- Core: 3–4 sets of 20–30 seconds

Session B
- Squats with pause or tempo: 4–5 sets of 5–8
- Split squats: 3–4 sets of 6–8 per leg
- Hip hinge: 4 sets of 8–12
- Core: 3–4 sets of 20–30 seconds

Session C
- Pull-up progression: 4–5 sets of 6–8
- Pressing pattern: push-up with elevated feet or more advanced incline if ready: 4 sets of 6–8
- Leg raises or hanging work: 4 sets of 8–12
- Core: rotational anti-movement drills

Session D
- Posterior chain: single-leg hip thrusts 4 sets of 8–12
- Glute bridge variations: 4 sets of 10–15
- Core stability: 3–4 sets of 20–40 seconds

Weekly progression and guidelines
- Reps to target each week:
  - Weeks 1–3: 8–12 reps per set for most exercises, higher reps on base movements
  - Weeks 4–6: 9–12 reps for main lifts, add an extra set where feasible
  - Weeks 7–9: 6–10 reps with tempo and controlled execution
  - Weeks 10–12: 5–8 reps with higher effort, near technical failure
- Sets: Start with 2–3 sets for most exercises in weeks 1–2; progress to 4 sets for main lifts by weeks 4–6 and maintain through weeks 12
- Rest between sets: 60–90 seconds for most exercises; 2–3 minutes for pull-ups or heavy holds if needed
- Pull-ups: use doorway bar as early as possible; if unable, do negative reps or inverted rows

Nutrition and recovery guidance
- Caloric needs: maintain a modest surplus if the goal is strength gain while ensuring adequate recovery; otherwise, maintain maintenance calories with sufficient protein
- Protein: aim for 1.6–2.2 g/kg of body weight per day to support muscle repair and growth
- Hydration: 2–3 liters per day
- Sleep: target 7–9 hours per night
- Post-workout nutrition: within 60–90 minutes of training, a mix of protein and carbohydrates (e.g., protein shake + fruit or yogurt + oats)
- Recovery practices: light activity on rest days (walks, mobility work), mobility sessions 10–15 minutes on off days

Progress tracking
- Record workouts: note exercise, sets, reps, tempo, and difficulty
- Track progression: aim to increase either reps, quality of movement, or duration of holds weekly
- Check-ins: every 4 weeks, reassess pull-up ability, push-up form, squat depth, and core stability

Safety notes
- Focus on technique first; quality over quantity
- If any pain (not normal muscle fatigue), stop and reassess form or reduce load
- Warm up thoroughly prior to each session; finish with cool-down and light mobility

It’s designed for a 27-year-old male, training at home with modest equipment, in a small flat. If you have his height/weight, I can tailor calories more precisely. For now, I’ll provide a flexible framework you can adapt.

Assumptions and goals
- Goal: lean muscle gain with strength improvements, while minimizing fat gain.
- Activity level: consistent 4 workouts/week as outlined.
- Estimated maintenance calories: a reasonable starting range for a typical healthy adult male is 2,500–2,900 kcal/day, but this can vary. Use a moderate surplus if his weight plateaus or for steady gains; or a maintenance rule if he wants minimal fat gain.
- Protein target: 1.6–2.2 g/kg body weight per day to support muscle repair and growth.
- Carbohydrates: provide energy for workouts and recovery; fats: support hormones and overall health.

Protein and macro targets
- Protein: 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight per day. For example, if he weighs 75 kg: 135–165 g protein/day.
- Fat: 0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight per day. Example: 60–75 g/day for 75 kg.
- Carbohydrates: fill remaining calories after protein and fat; prioritize timing around workouts.
- Fiber: aim for 25–35 g/day from vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes.

Meal timing and structure
- Eat 3 main meals with 1–2 snacks as needed to hit protein and caloric targets.
- Pre-workout: a small carb-focused snack 60–90 minutes before training if appetite allows (e.g., banana, yogurt, oats).
- Post-workout: a rapid-protein, moderate-carb option within 60–90 minutes (e.g., protein shake with a fruit, or chicken/egg with rice and vegetables).
- Hydration: 2–3 liters of water per day; consider electrolytes if workouts are long or very sweaty.

Sample daily structure (adjust portions to hit targets)
- Breakfast: protein-rich + complex carbs + vegetables
  - Example: 3 eggs or 1 cup egg whites + 1 whole egg, 1 cup cooked oats or 2 slices whole-grain toast, fruit, spinach or berries
- Lunch: protein + starch + veg + healthy fats
  - Example: 150–200 g grilled chicken or tofu, 1–1.5 cups cooked rice or quinoa, large salad with olive oil, veggies
- Snack: protein + fruit or yogurt + nuts
  - Example: Greek yogurt 200 g + fruit; or whey protein shake + apple + a handful of almonds
- Dinner: protein + vegetables + optional starch
  - Example: 150–200 g lean beef, fish, or tempeh; huge veggie portion; sweet potato or whole grain pasta if appetite allows
- Optional post-dinner snack (if needed for calories/protein): cottage cheese, casein protein, or a small handful of nuts

Calorie adjustment framework
- Week 1–4: Start with a modest surplus if weight goals are to gain muscle; 250–350 kcal above maintenance on training days
- Week 5–12: Reassess every 4 weeks
  - If weight is increasing by about 0.25–0.5 kg/week, this is a good pace; adjust up or down by 100–200 kcal depending on progress
  - If weight is stable and strength is increasing, keep calories around maintenance with high protein
  - If fat gain is a concern, reduce overall calories by 150–300 kcal on non-training days or slightly reduce carbs

Micronutrients and food quality
- Emphasize whole foods: lean proteins, eggs, dairy or alternatives, beans, lentils, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, healthy fats (olive oil, avocado).
- Include colorful vegetables at every meal for micronutrients and fiber.
- Limit highly processed foods, added sugars, and sugary beverages.

Meal timing example for training days (adjust to schedule)
- Pre-workout meal 60–90 minutes before: 1 cup oats with milk or water + a scoop of protein; or whole-grain toast with peanut butter + banana
- Post-workout meal within 60–90 minutes: 25–40 g protein + 60–80 g carbs (e.g., protein shake + banana, or chicken with rice and vegetables)
- If training later in the day, you can move some carbs to post-workout and keep protein steady

Week-by-week nutrition adjustments (alignment with training phases)
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): establish protein intake and habit; eat roughly maintenance plus 250 kcal on training days if aiming for gains; emphasize protein in every meal; ensure hydration
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): monitor weight and performance; adjust calories if weight loss/plateau or rapid gain occurs; continue consistent protein intake
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): if intensifying lifts, maintain or slightly increase calories to sustain recovery; keep protein high; ensure carb intake supports workouts
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): fine-tune to maintain strength gains with minimal fat gain; shift to maintenance or slight surplus depending on goals

Tracking and accountability
- Use a simple log (app or notebook):
  - Daily calories, protein, carbs, fats
  - Weight once per week, ideally same time of day
  - Training performance: reps completed, perceived effort, any issues
- Adjust weekly based on progress:
  - If gaining too fast (>0.3–0.5 kg/week) and the client wants to limit fat gain, reduce calories by 150–250 kcal on non-training days
  - If not gaining after 2–3 weeks, add about 150–200 kcal on training days

Allergen-free or dietary preferences
- If he’s vegetarian/vegan, substitute animal protein with plant-based sources (lentils, beans, tofu, tempeh, seitan, dairy or fortified alternatives) and adjust protein targets accordingly (potentially higher volume or supplemental protein powder).
- If he has lactose intolerance or other restrictions, choose lactose-free dairy options or yogurt alternatives; ensure protein targets are met.

Practical tips for a small flat
- Use a shopping list with versatile protein sources (eggs, chicken thighs, canned tuna, beans, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, tofu).
- Batch-cook on weekends: grill or bake a batch of chicken, rice or potatoes, roasted veggies; portion into containers for quick meals.

- Why: Versatile for all major lifts (lunges, goblet squats, dumbbell rows, overhead press when possible, Romanian deadlifts, farmer carries if you upgrade later).

2) Kettlebell (optional alternative to dumbbells)
- If space is extremely limited or if he prefers single-sided loading, a single adjustable kettlebell can work.

How to choose based on goals and space
- Budget-conscious and space-limited: Start with a pair of adjustable dumbbells (5–20 kg) or a kettlebell in the 8–16 kg range, plus a couple resistance bands. These cover most transitions from Phase 2 to Phase 4 in the program.

Practical progression plan for equipment use
- Weeks 1–4 (Phase 1–early Phase 2): Rely on bodyweight; introduce light resistance only if absolutely necessary for progression (e.g., goblet squat with a 10–15 lb dumbbell, light goblet hold for squats, light dumbbell rows).
- Weeks 5–8: Add weight progressively:

  - Dumbbell rows or incline dumbbell presses with light-to-moderate weights.
  - Romanian deadlifts with dumbbells, starting light and moving heavier as technique allows.
- Weeks 9–12 and beyond: Target heavier loads for main lifts (e.g., dumbbell presses, rows, goblet squats, hip hinge movements) while keeping sets/reps aligned with phase goals. Consider adding a second pair of heavier dumbbells or increasing kettlebell weight if needed.

Safety and practicality tips
- Movement first: Ensure technique is solid before increasing weight. Use slower tempos and longer rests if form degrades.
- Floor protection: Use a mat or thick towel on hard floors for comfort, especially during deadlifts and floor work.
- Storage: Keep equipment in a dedicated corner or under the bed to minimize space usage and noise.
- Noise considerations: If apartment buildings have strict noise rules, emphasize slow/controlled reps, tempo work, and non-joint-impact movements (no heavy drop sets).

- Arm circles: 10–12 reps forward and backward each arm
- Hip circles: 6–8 in each direction per hip

Mobility sequence (12–14 minutes)
1) Thoracic spine openers (3 rounds)
- Wall thoracic rotations: stand next to wall, place forearm on wall, rotate chest toward wall. 6–8 reps per side.
- Open-book stretch (on side): 8–10 reps per side, focusing on ribcage rotation and scapular movement.

2) Shoulders and chest neutrality (2–3 rounds)
- Doorway lat stretch: stand in doorway, 90/90 elbow at side, step forward to feel stretch across chest and front shoulder. Hold 20–30 seconds per side.

- Scapular squeezes: stand or sit tall, squeeze shoulder blades together and down for 6–8 seconds; rest 4–6 seconds; x8 reps.

- Diaphragmatic breathing: 6 breaths to 4–6 seconds inhale, 4–6 seconds exhale; focus on rib cage expansion.

- Light forward fold or child’s pose to reset nervous system
- Gentle neck circles and shoulder rolls, 5–6 each direction
